title: Glossary
markdown:
Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A\*** | Shortest-path search ordered by f = g + h, where h estimates the remaining cost to the goal. (5.05) |
| **Adaptive** | Doing less work on easier inputs, as insertion sort does on nearly sorted data. (3.01) |
| **Adjacency list** | A graph stored as a list of neighbours for each vertex: O(V + E) memory. (5.01) |
| **Adjacency matrix** | A graph stored as a V × V table of edges: O(V²) memory, O(1) edge test. (5.01) |
| **Admissible heuristic** | An estimate that never overestimates the true remaining cost, so A* stays optimal. (5.05) |
| **Amortised cost** | The average cost per operation over any sequence of operations, such as O(1) for `push_back`. (1.01) |
| **Augmenting a structure** | Storing extra data in each node (subtree size, sum) to answer new questions. (4.02) |
| **AVL tree** | A self-balancing BST in which every node's subtree heights differ by at most one. (4.03) |
| **Backtracking** | Building a solution choice by choice, abandoning partial solutions that cannot succeed. (6.05) |
| **Balance factor** | The height of a node's left subtree minus that of its right subtree. (4.03) |
| **BFS (breadth-first search)** | Exploring a graph in layers with a queue; finds fewest-edge paths. (5.01) |
| **Big O** | An upper bound on how a cost grows with the input size, ignoring constants. (1.01) |
| **Binary heap** | A complete binary tree in an array where every parent is at least (or at most) its children. (3.04) |
| **Binary search** | Finding a value in sorted data by halving the range: O(log n). (2.01) |
| **Binary search tree (BST)** | A binary tree with smaller keys to the left and larger keys to the right of every node. (4.02) |
| **Bipartite graph** | A graph whose vertices split into two groups with every edge between the groups. (5.01) |
| **Branch and bound** | Backtracking that prunes partial solutions whose best possible result cannot beat the best found. (6.05) |
| **Bucket** | One slot of a hash table, selected by `hash % bucketCount`. (2.02) |
| **Cache line** | The 64-byte block in which memory moves between RAM and the caches. (1.02) |
| **Chaining** | Handling hash collisions by keeping a list of entries in each bucket. (2.03) |
| **Collision** | Two different keys landing in the same bucket. (2.02) |
| **Comparator** | A function `less(a, b)` defining an order; it must be a strict weak ordering. (3.01) |
| **Complete binary tree** | A tree whose levels are all full except possibly the last, filled from the left. (3.04) |
| **Connected component** | A maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other. (5.01) |
| **Consistent heuristic** | A heuristic with h(u) ≤ w(u, v) + h(v) for every edge; each vertex is then expanded once. (5.05) |
| **Counting sort** | Sorting small integer keys by counting each value: O(n + k). (3.05) |
| **Cycle** | A path that returns to its starting vertex. (5.01) |
| **DAG** | A directed acyclic graph: directed edges and no cycles. (5.02) |
| **Deque** | A double-ended queue: O(1) push and pop at both ends. (1.05) |
| **DFS (depth-first search)** | Exploring a graph by going as deep as possible before backtracking. (5.02) |
| **Dijkstra's algorithm** | Shortest paths with non-negative weights, finishing vertices in order of distance with a heap. (5.03) |
| **Divide and conquer** | Splitting a problem into smaller copies, solving them, and combining the answers. (3.02) |
| **Dynamic array** | A contiguous array that grows by reallocating, like `std::vector`. (1.03) |
| **Dynamic programming** | Solving overlapping subproblems once each and storing the answers. (6.02) |
| **Edit distance** | The fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions turning one string into another. (6.03) |
| **Exchange argument** | Proving a greedy algorithm correct by transforming any optimal solution into the greedy one. (6.01) |
| **Fenwick tree** | An array of block sums sized by the lowest set bit: O(log n) updates and prefix sums. (4.04) |
| **Greedy algorithm** | Building a solution by always taking the locally best choice. (6.01) |
| **Hash function** | A function turning a key into a number; equal keys must give equal hashes. (2.02) |
| **Hash table** | A table that finds keys by hashing them to buckets: expected O(1) operations. (2.03) |
| **Heapsort** | Sorting by building a heap and repeatedly moving its root to the end: O(n log n), in place. (3.04) |
| **Height** | The number of edges on the longest path from a node down to a leaf. (4.01) |
| **In-order traversal** | Left subtree, node, right subtree; visits a BST's keys in sorted order. (4.01) |
| **In place** | Using only O(1) (or O(log n)) extra memory. (3.01) |
| **Insertion sort** | Inserting each element into the sorted prefix before it: O(n + inversions). (3.01) |
| **Introsort** | Quicksort that switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep, and insertion sort for small parts; `std::sort`. (3.03) |
| **Invariant** | A fact that holds before and after every step of a loop, used to reason about correctness. (2.01) |
| **Inversion** | A pair of positions whose elements are in the wrong order. (3.01) |
| **Kahn's algorithm** | Topological sorting by repeatedly removing vertices with in-degree zero. (5.02) |
| **KMP** | The Knuth-Morris-Pratt string search, using the prefix function to never re-read text: O(n + m). (6.04) |
| **Kruskal's algorithm** | A minimum spanning tree from edges taken cheapest first, skipping those that close a cycle. (5.04) |
| **Lazy deletion** | Leaving outdated heap entries in place and skipping them when popped. (5.03) |
| **Linear probing** | Open addressing that tries the following slots one by one. (2.04) |
| **Linked list** | A sequence of nodes, each pointing to the next (and, if doubly linked, the previous). (1.04) |
| **Load factor** | Entries divided by buckets (or slots) in a hash table. (2.03) |
| **Longest common subsequence** | The longest sequence appearing in order (not necessarily contiguously) in two strings. (6.03) |
| **Longest increasing subsequence** | The longest strictly increasing subsequence; O(n log n) by patience sorting. (6.03) |
| **Lower bound** | The first position whose value is at least the target. (2.01) |
| **Master theorem** | Solves recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(nᵈ) by comparing a with bᵈ. (3.02) |
| **Memoisation** | Caching the results of a recursive function so each input is computed once. (6.02) |
| **Merge sort** | Sort both halves, then merge them: O(n log n), stable, needs a buffer. (3.02) |
| **Minimum spanning tree** | The cheapest set of edges connecting all vertices, with no cycles. (5.04) |
| **Monotonic deque** | A deque kept in sorted order, giving sliding-window maxima in O(n). (1.05) |
| **NP-complete** | A problem whose solutions are easy to check but for which no fast algorithm is known. (6.05) |
| **Open addressing** | Storing hash entries in the array itself and probing for free slots. (2.04) |
| **Partition** | Rearranging elements around a pivot: smaller before, larger after. (3.03) |
| **Path compression** | Pointing every node on a union-find path directly at the root. (4.05) |
| **Pivot** | The element quicksort partitions around. (3.03) |
| **Prefix function** | For each position, the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix there. (6.04) |
| **Prefix sums** | Running totals that answer range sums in O(1) for unchanging data. (4.04) |
| **Prim's algorithm** | A minimum spanning tree grown from one vertex by always adding the cheapest attaching edge. (5.04) |
| **Priority queue** | A collection that always hands out its highest-priority element next. (3.04) |
| **Quickselect** | Finding the k-th smallest element by partitioning and recursing into one side: expected O(n). (3.03) |
| **Quicksort** | Partition around a pivot, then sort each side: O(n log n) on average. (3.03) |
| **Radix sort** | Sorting digit by digit with a stable counting sort: O(d(n + b)). (3.05) |
| **Rehashing** | Moving every entry into a bigger table when the load factor gets too high. (2.03) |
| **Relaxation** | Improving a vertex's distance via an edge: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v]. (5.03) |
| **Ring buffer** | A fixed array used as a queue with wrap-around indexes. (1.05) |
| **Rolling hash** | A hash of a sliding window updated in O(1) per step. (2.02) |
| **Rotation** | A local restructuring of a node and its child that keeps BST order. (4.03) |
| **Segment tree** | A tree storing the answer for every segment of a recursive halving: O(log n) range queries and updates. (4.04) |
| **Sentinel** | A dummy node that removes special cases, such as at the ends of a list. (1.04) |
| **Shunting-yard algorithm** | Evaluating expressions with an operator stack and a value stack. (1.05) |
| **Stable sort** | A sort that keeps equal elements in their original order. (3.01) |
| **Stack** | A last-in, first-out collection. (1.05) |
| **Strict weak ordering** | The rules a comparator must obey: irreflexive, transitive, with transitive equivalence. (3.01) |
| **Tabulation** | Filling a dynamic-programming table with loops in a safe order. (6.02) |
| **Tombstone** | A marker left by erasing from an open-addressing table so probes continue past it. (2.04) |
| **Topological order** | An order of a DAG's vertices in which every edge points forward. (5.02) |
| **Trie** | A tree that stores strings character by character; prefix queries in O(length). (6.04) |
| **Union-find** | A forest of parent pointers tracking disjoint sets under merging, in near O(1) per operation. (4.05) |
| **Union by size** | Attaching the smaller tree under the larger one in union-find. (4.05) |
